b: Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than altering the community of bacteria living in your gut. New research suggests that drinking coffee regularly may also influence the way the digestive system itself functions, from the acidity of the small intestine to the muscular contractions that move material through the colon.

To investigate these effects, scientists at the University of Copenhagen used a small electronic capsule that participants swallowed. As the device made its way through the digestive tract, it collected data on several aspects of gut function, including how quickly material traveled through the gastrointestinal system, temperature, acidity, and intestinal contractions.

The researchers divided participants into two groups based on their coffee consumption. Frequent coffee drinkers were defined as those who consumed between one and five cups per day on more than three of the eight days during which dietary intake was recorded. The remaining participants drank coffee less frequently.

Consistent with earlier research, the team found a link between coffee consumption and the composition of the gut microbiome. People who drank coffee frequently had a greater diversity of gut microorganisms than those who consumed it less often.

"But perhaps more importantly, frequent coffee consumption appears to affect the physiology of the gut itself, in other words how the gut functions," says first author Francesca Bucci, a PhD student at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports at the University of Copenhagen.

Previous studies have established associations between moderate coffee consumption and a lower risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, depression, and several forms of cancer. Yet relatively little is known about how regular coffee consumption relates to the physical and chemical conditions inside the digestive tract.
Coffee Linked to Increased Intestinal Activity

One of the most notable findings was that frequent coffee drinkers had significantly more acidic conditions in their small intestine, as indicated by a lower pH. Greater coffee consumption was also associated with an increased number of muscular contractions in the colon.
These contractions play an essential role in moving material through the digestive system. The findings raise the possibility that regular coffee consumption could help support this natural process.
"Contractions in the gut can support healthy digestion, help prevent constipation and keep the intestinal muscles in good condition," says Francesca Bucci.

Whether the increased acidity in the small intestine has positive or negative consequences for health remains unclear. Acidity is an important factor in digestion because it influences how digestive enzymes function and how effectively food is broken down.
Could Coffee Be Driving These Changes?

Because the study was observational, the researchers cannot establish whether coffee itself was entirely responsible for the differences they detected. However, senior study author Henrik Munch Roager points out that previous research provides several reasons to suspect that coffee contributes to these changes.

"For example, we already know from other studies that coffee can influence a range of processes in the digestive system, including acid secretion in the stomach. So there are good reasons to believe that what we are seeing is not merely coincidence. Anecdotally, many people also report that coffee affects their digestion," says Henrik Munch Roager, Associate Professor and Research Group Leader at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports.
A Potential Natural Way To Improve Gut Motility

Roager says the next logical step would be to conduct a controlled intervention study. By regulating participants' coffee intake, scientists could compare digestive function during periods of high coffee consumption with periods when participants avoid coffee altogether.

Such an experiment could help clarify whether coffee directly influences gut physiology and whether its effects could be harnessed to address common digestive complaints, including constipation and irregular bowel movements.

"A great many people struggle with constipation and irregular bowel movements. If we can understand how coffee affects digestion and intestinal contractions, it may be possible to use that knowledge to stimulate gut motility in a natural way. That would be extremely valuable," says Henrik Munch Roager.
The study involved 61 healthy adults from Denmark and was published in Gut Microbiology.

Of those participants, 50 swallowed a SmartPill®, a wireless electronic capsule that transmitted data as it moved through the gastrointestinal tract. The device recorded transit time, acidity (pH), temperature, pressure, and intestinal contractions.
The research was conducted over nine consecutive days.
Participants kept detailed records of everything they ate and drank for eight days, providing researchers with information about their overall diets and coffee consumption.
To obtain an objective indicator of coffee intake, the scientists also analyzed urine samples for caffeine metabolites, substances produced when the body breaks down caffeine.
Researchers collected and analyzed stool samples to determine the composition and abundance of microorganisms in the gut.
The team used these measurements to examine associations between coffee consumption, the gut microbiome, and the physiological functioning of the digestive system.
